# A Quick Return to the Tidyverse {background-color="#007155"}

## Wide vs. Long Data {.smaller}

```{r}
bea_wide <- tibble(
  county_name = c("Addison, VT", "Chittenden, VT", "Rutland, VT"),
  pop_2020 = c(37363, 168323, 60572),
  pop_2021 = c(37162, 169660, 60381),
  pop_2022 = c(36777, 170533, 59949)
)

bea_wide
```

- One row per county, but each year gets its own column
- This is what you get if you ever download **multiple years** from BEA at
  once, instead of the single year HW2 asked for

## `pivot_longer()`: Wide to Long {.smaller}

```{r}
bea_long <- bea_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("pop_"),
    names_to = "year",
    names_prefix = "pop_",
    values_to = "population"
  )

bea_long
```

- One row per county *and* year, instead of one row per county
- Almost everything in dplyr and ggplot2 wants data in this shape
- `names_prefix` strips `"pop_"` so the year column just holds the number

## `pivot_wider()`: The Reverse {.smaller}

```{r}
bea_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = population)
```

- Takes values from one column and spreads them into new columns, one per
  unique value
- Good for a summary table you want to read by eye, less useful once you
  need to filter or group by year again


# Getting Data {background-color="#007155"}

## Where Data Comes From {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="70%"}
- A file someone hands you, or you download: CSV, Excel, and the like
- A live API (application programming interface) you query with code
- A web page you scrape, when nothing else is available
- R4DS Ch. 7-8 covers the first in depth. APIs and scraping are in R4DS
  [Ch. 24](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/webscraping.html), much further along in
  the book than we've gotten
- Reading files is `readr`'s job, the tidyverse package behind `read_csv()` and other similar functions
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](https://readr.tidyverse.org/logo.png)
:::

::::

## Reading Files, Revisited {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
read_csv(
  "data/hw2a.csv",
  skip = 3,
  na = c("", "NA", "(NA)", "N/A")
)
```

- `read_csv()` is in HW2's starter code
- `skip` jumps past header rows a file doesn't need, common in government
  exports
- `na` tells readr which strings actually mean "missing." This varies widely.
- `readr` prints a column specification when it loads. Always glance at it. A
  date or number read in as text usually means a stray character snuck into
  that column


# Getting Data from an API {background-color="#007155"}

## What's an API? {.smaller}

- **Application programming interface**: structured way to ask a website for data and get back something other than a webpage, usually JSON
- You build a URL with your request baked in, and the server sends back
  data instead of a rendered page
- Census, BLS, and BEA all publish APIs. Some want a free registration key, a few don't

## Not Every API Is Free {.smaller}

- There is an entire industry based around data for purchase. For example, you might want to get a drive distance from UVM campus to 500 different addresses in Vermont. You could get this for free by manually entering the addresses into Google Maps. Or you could give Google a single file with every address and have it calculate all 500 distances in a few minutes.
- **The catch**: you have to pay! (a fraction of a penny for each, but it adds up)
- If a private data provider gives you an API key, keep it secret or bad actors can drain your credits (or wallet) in a very short time.

## A Live Example: the BLS API {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(jsonlite)

url <- "https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/LNS14000000"
bls_raw <- fromJSON(url)
bls_raw

bls_raw$Results$series$data[[1]] |> head()
```

- `LNS14000000` is the BLS series ID for the national unemployment rate
- No key needed for a request this small, heavier use wants a free one
- `fromJSON()` already turned the nested JSON into data frames. We just have to dig through the list to find the one we want
- Read `bls_raw$Results$series$data[[1]]` left to right: start at `bls_raw`,
  step into `$Results`, then `$series`, then grab the first item out of the
  `data` list with `[[1]]`

## Turning It Into a Tidy Data Frame {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
unemployment <- bls_raw$Results$series$data[[1]] |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(year, period, value) |>
  mutate(value = as.numeric(value))

unemployment
```

- `$` and `[[ ]]` dig through the nested list until you hit the data frame
  you actually want
- Watch `value` after the conversion: one row comes back `NA`, from the
  month of the 2025 government shutdown. Real missing data, not a mistake
- Week 8's `tidycensus` wraps this same fetch-then-dig pattern, but for
  Census data specifically. It will become our friend. 

## Web Scraping: A Quick Look {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(rvest)

page <- read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_counties_in_Vermont")
counties <- page |>
  html_element("table.wikitable") |>
  html_table()
```

- Some data only exists inside a web page, with no file or API behind it
- `rvest` reads a page's HTML and pulls out a specific table or element
- **The process is fragile**: if the page's layout changes, your code breaks with no warning
- Use it last, after checking for a file or an API. Read the site's terms of
  service and `robots.txt` first, and never hit a server with rapid repeated
  requests, it can look like an attack and get you blocked

# Joins: Combining Two Data Frames {background-color="#007155"}

## Why Joins {.smaller}

- HW2 step 5 asks you to combine `df` and `df2` using a shared column,
  `county_fips`
- A join lines up rows from two tables using one or more shared columns,
  called **keys** (we will often refer to this as a "unique identifier")
- Nothing here is BEA-specific. Joins work the same way on any two data
  frames that share a key

![](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/diagrams/join/venn.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

## A Small Example {.smaller}

```{r}
pop <- tibble(
  county_fips = c("50001", "50003", "50007"),
  county_name = c("Addison", "Bennington", "Chittenden"),
  population = c(37363, 34478, 168323)
)

income <- tibble(
  county_fips = c("50001", "50003", "50011"),
  income = c(58000, 52000, 71000)
)
```

- Both tables share `county_fips`, the key
- The counties don't fully overlap: 50007 is only in `pop`, 50011 only in
  `income`

## `left_join()`: Keep Everything on the Left {.smaller}

```{r}
pop |> left_join(income, by = "county_fips")
```

- Every row of `pop` survives, matched or not
- Chittenden (50007) has no match in `income`, so it gets `NA`
- 50011's income is dropped. It wasn't in `pop` to begin with

## Other Join Types, Briefly

| Join | Keeps |
|---|---|
| `left_join()` | Everything on the left, matched where possible |
| `inner_join()` | Only rows that match in both |
| `full_join()` | Everything from both, matched where possible |

`left_join()` is the one you'll reach for almost every time: you have a main
table and you're adding to it.

## Watch Out: Duplicate Column Names {.smaller}

- If both tables have a column with the same name that isn't the key (both
  have `county_name`, say), the join keeps both and adds `.x` and `.y`
  suffixes
- Two fixes:
  - `select()` away the extra column from one side before joining
  - Join on every shared column: `by = c("county_fips", "county_name", "state")`

## A Bigger Example: `nycflights13` {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("nycflights13")  # once, if you don't already have it
```

```{r}
library(nycflights13)

flights |> select(year, month, day, carrier, flight, dest)
```

- The same package R4DS's [joins chapter](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/joins.html)
  uses: every flight that left a NYC airport in 2013
- `carrier` is a two-letter code, not an airline name, exactly the kind of
  gap a join fills

## The Lookup Table: `airlines` {.smaller}

```{r}
airlines
```

- One row per code, the exact shape you want on the right side of a
  `left_join()`
- Same key idea as `pop` and `income`: both tables share a column,
  `carrier`

## Joining Them {.smaller}

```{r}
flights |>
  select(year, month, day, carrier, flight, dest) |>
  left_join(airlines, by = "carrier")
```

- Same `left_join()`, same idea as `pop` and `income`, just bigger, real
  data
- Every flight keeps its row. It just gains the airline's full name

## Your Turn: One Way to Do It {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
# 1
pop |> inner_join(income, by = "county_fips")
# Only 2 rows: just the counties present in both tables

# 2
bea_long |>
  group_by(county_name) |>
  mutate(change = population - lag(population)) |>
  filter(!is.na(change))

# 3
flights |>
  left_join(airlines, by = "carrier") |>
  count(name, sort = TRUE)
```
